Right to his final act, Smith is proving to be the consummate professor, giving us a valuable master class on faith and life. Each anecdote is offered up with minimum explication and just a few choice adjectives, as if Smith's sense of marvel at the strange bounty of the world should suffice. And in most cases, it does. result.features: Already renowned as a statesman, Thomas Jefferson in his retirement from government turned his attention to the founding of an institution of higher learning. Never merely a patron, the former president oversaw every aspect of the creation of what would become the University of Virginia. Along with the Declaration of Independence and the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, he regarded it as one of the three greatest achievements in his life. Nonetheless, historians often treat this period as an epilogue to Jefferson’s career. In The Illimitable Freedom of the Human Mind, Andrew O’Shaughnessy offers a twin biography of Jefferson in retirement and of the University of Virginia in its earliest years. He reveals how Jefferson’s vision anticipated the modern university and profoundly influenced the development of American higher education. The University of Virginia was the most visible apex of what was a much broader educational vision that distinguishes Jefferson as one of the earliest advocates of a public education system. Just as Jefferson’s proclamation that "all men are created equal" was tainted by the ongoing institution of slavery, however, so was his university. O’Shaughnessy addresses this tragic conflict in Jefferson’s conception of the university and society, showing how Jefferson’s loftier aspirations for the university were not fully realized. Nevertheless, his remarkable vision in founding the university remains vital to any consideration of the role of education in the success of the democratic experiment.

top_reviews.title: One of the best books on the mind of Thomas Jefferson
top_reviews.text:
Although this book's principal focus is Jefferson's role in conceiving and bringing into existence the University of Virginia,the author wisely concludes he must explore TJ's general philosophy and values as part of that process. And the author knows of what he speaks as an officer of the Jefferson foundation at Monticello and a distinguished historian, probably best known for his "The Men Who Lost America."

Jefferson is well known as a child of the Enlightenment, determined to remove all barriers to knowledge. His mastery with the pen, be it the Declaration, the Virginia Statute of Religious Freedom, or the Notes on Virginia, is well established. He was a true product of the Scottish Enlightenment, French thought, as well as science. We must add the title of "educational reformer" as well. Whereas up to ten years or so ago, most historians worked hard to avoid linking TJ to slavery, one need only take a look at the NY City Council expulsion of his statue to see why, this author makes repeated references to it and devotes a superior chapter just to that topic. That chapter lays it all out and I found it a bit disturbing even though I have studied TJ for many decades.

The central theme of the book is the unbelievable efforts Jefferson had to undergo to bring UVA into existence in 1819. In addition to legislators who were stingy with funds, other Virginia leaders who wanted the university situated anywhere but Charlottesville, the entire religious establishment rained abuse on to a university that would have no religious instruction, no ministers, no chapel, and would close it facilities to religious usages. But Jefferson would simply not compromise to any extent on this. Fortunately, Madison supported him. Interestingly, the author disputes any contention that the major purpose of UVA for TJ was to protect impressionable young southern gentlemen from northern abolitionism at places like Princeton. This point I remain unconvinced on.

Jefferson not only created UVA, but put his significant architectural talents to work designing the buildings and the layout of the famous "architectural village."He also designed the curriculum (later copied at many colleges), hired the faculty from mostly Britain, and selected the books for the library. I have a 1945 UVA publication that lists the 6500 books originally in the Rotunda, many selected and even shelved by Jefferson. Any Federalist or Tory (e.g., Blackstone) advocates had their writings excluded. "Useful knowledge" was the key.

Trying to trace Jefferson's thinking on slavery, abolition, or the capabilities of Anglo-Americans is like following the proverbial trail of breadcrumbs through the woods. He is all over the map, changes his positions at key junctures, and eventually contents himself with writing tracts on "states' rights." The author has written the best analysis of all these gradations, refinements, and chicanery that I have seen in 50 years. I don't know if he answers all questions, if anyone could, but he certainly enlightens the reader. For me there was a lot of pain, but also some good, and it is definitely a mixed picture.

The text is supported with 54 wonderful illustrations and 55 helpful notes. Its 308 pages are just fascinating to read, and cover the early 19th century politics as well as Jefferson. One of the finest volumes in the Jefferson literature.

top_reviews.title: University of Virginla
top_reviews.text:
If you're an admirer of Thomas Jefferson (his mind not his morals!) you'll love how he decided to create a university. Jefferson was always THINKING; using his prodigious mind and especially how it can benefit the state of Virginia. While he admired the University of William and Mary, in his later years he wanted a university that could educate the best and brightest (men) of Virginia to benefit humanity. He always felt education was the only way this grand experiment would succeed. Fortunately he lived long enough to see his dream become a reality.
This is a wonderful book about Jefferson's later years and his belief in education especially for Virginia.

result.features: Already renowned as a statesman, Thomas Jefferson in his retirement from government turned his attention to the founding of an institution of higher learning. Never merely a patron, the former president oversaw every aspect of the creation of what would become the University of Virginia. Along with the Declaration of Independence and the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, he regarded it as one of the three greatest achievements in his life. Nonetheless, historians often treat this period as an epilogue to Jefferson’s career. In The Illimitable Freedom of the Human Mind, Andrew O’Shaughnessy offers a twin biography of Jefferson in retirement and of the University of Virginia in its earliest years. He reveals how Jefferson’s vision anticipated the modern university and profoundly influenced the development of American higher education. The University of Virginia was the most visible apex of what was a much broader educational vision that distinguishes Jefferson as one of the earliest advocates of a public education system. Just as Jefferson’s proclamation that "all men are created equal" was tainted by the ongoing institution of slavery, however, so was his university. O’Shaughnessy addresses this tragic conflict in Jefferson’s conception of the university and society, showing how Jefferson’s loftier aspirations for the university were not fully realized. Nevertheless, his remarkable vision in founding the university remains vital to any consideration of the role of education in the success of the democratic experiment.

top_reviews.title: One of the best books on the mind of Thomas Jefferson
top_reviews.text:
Although this book's principal focus is Jefferson's role in conceiving and bringing into existence the University of Virginia,the author wisely concludes he must explore TJ's general philosophy and values as part of that process. And the author knows of what he speaks as an officer of the Jefferson foundation at Monticello and a distinguished historian, probably best known for his "The Men Who Lost America."

Jefferson is well known as a child of the Enlightenment, determined to remove all barriers to knowledge. His mastery with the pen, be it the Declaration, the Virginia Statute of Religious Freedom, or the Notes on Virginia, is well established. He was a true product of the Scottish Enlightenment, French thought, as well as science. We must add the title of "educational reformer" as well. Whereas up to ten years or so ago, most historians worked hard to avoid linking TJ to slavery, one need only take a look at the NY City Council expulsion of his statue to see why, this author makes repeated references to it and devotes a superior chapter just to that topic. That chapter lays it all out and I found it a bit disturbing even though I have studied TJ for many decades.

The central theme of the book is the unbelievable efforts Jefferson had to undergo to bring UVA into existence in 1819. In addition to legislators who were stingy with funds, other Virginia leaders who wanted the university situated anywhere but Charlottesville, the entire religious establishment rained abuse on to a university that would have no religious instruction, no ministers, no chapel, and would close it facilities to religious usages. But Jefferson would simply not compromise to any extent on this. Fortunately, Madison supported him. Interestingly, the author disputes any contention that the major purpose of UVA for TJ was to protect impressionable young southern gentlemen from northern abolitionism at places like Princeton. This point I remain unconvinced on.

Jefferson not only created UVA, but put his significant architectural talents to work designing the buildings and the layout of the famous "architectural village."He also designed the curriculum (later copied at many colleges), hired the faculty from mostly Britain, and selected the books for the library. I have a 1945 UVA publication that lists the 6500 books originally in the Rotunda, many selected and even shelved by Jefferson. Any Federalist or Tory (e.g., Blackstone) advocates had their writings excluded. "Useful knowledge" was the key.

Trying to trace Jefferson's thinking on slavery, abolition, or the capabilities of Anglo-Americans is like following the proverbial trail of breadcrumbs through the woods. He is all over the map, changes his positions at key junctures, and eventually contents himself with writing tracts on "states' rights." The author has written the best analysis of all these gradations, refinements, and chicanery that I have seen in 50 years. I don't know if he answers all questions, if anyone could, but he certainly enlightens the reader. For me there was a lot of pain, but also some good, and it is definitely a mixed picture.

The text is supported with 54 wonderful illustrations and 55 helpful notes. Its 308 pages are just fascinating to read, and cover the early 19th century politics as well as Jefferson. One of the finest volumes in the Jefferson literature.

top_reviews.text:
If you're an admirer of Thomas Jefferson (his mind not his morals!) you'll love how he decided to create a university. Jefferson was always THINKING; using his prodigious mind and especially how it can benefit the state of Virginia. While he admired the University of William and Mary, in his later years he wanted a university that could educate the best and brightest (men) of Virginia to benefit humanity. He always felt education was the only way this grand experiment would succeed. Fortunately he lived long enough to see his dream become a reality.
This is a wonderful book about Jefferson's later years and his belief in education especially for Virginia.

Watson lives in Chico, California. Excerpt. © Reprinted by permission. All rights reserved. WEDNESDAY, MARCH 25 TECHIES Theo had never made out with a girl before. He’d kissed his date good night after the winter formal last December, and for a couple of weeks in junior high he went steady with Paisley Reed. But this was different. This was lying-on-the-bed different. Theo thought he might be in love. Maggie rolled onto her back and Theo flopped beside her. Taking a break was probably a good thing because at the moment, he was so turned on he could barely move. “I really liked your movie,” she whispered. He shrugged, a little wary about having shown his video footage to her. “It’s not finished yet,” he told her. “What do you mean?” He frowned. “I still have a few scores to settle.” Maggie laughed. “Interesting choice of words. Is that how you settle your scores? On film?” Theo turned his head, reaching over to stroke Maggie’s hair behind her ear. “You know a better way?” he teased. He decided to make his point by pulling his video camera out of his pocket and turning it on. Maggie stared into the lens. “No,” she said, unsmiling. He leaned up on one elbow, focused in tight on her face. “No, what?” he asked. “You don’t want me to film you? Or no, you don’t know a better way?” She kept watching him, her eyes burning into his viewfinder. “Maybe.” “Maybe what?” he asked, a little surprised. She held her gaze on the tiny screen. “Maybe I have some scores of my own to settle. Maybe I have my own way of settling them.” Theo’s heart sped up. “With who?” She shrugged. “I dunno. Jocks. Preps. People who are out to get people like us.” Theo’s head whirled. He was almost positive by now that he loved this girl. It was like she could read his thoughts—like they’d lived inside each other’s heads their whole lives. “Why are preps and jocks out to get you?” he asked, narrowing in on Maggie’s intense eyes. She blinked into the lens a few times. “Because they can’t see beyond the package,” she whispered. Theo paused. What had started out as an amusing diversion was taking on an entirely darker dimension. He could sense something bubbling under the surface of Maggie’s skin, a reckoning of some kind. He wasn’t afraid of it; he actually wanted to explore it. “What can’t they see?” he asked, just above a whisper. “Intellect,” she said. “Heart. Soul. Danger.” “What kind of danger?” Her hair fell forward, leaving only one blue eye visible behind a chestnut curtain. “The kind of thing that happens when they push too far without realizing.” Read more
